label: Earth science / geologic hazards
description: The teams that monitor, forecast and warn for earthquakes, volcanoes, tsunamis and landslides, and the partners who act on their warnings. Four variants share one profile: a volcano observatory (alert levels, aviation color codes, notices to emergency management and aviation), a seismic network with earthquake early warning operations (event solutions, ShakeMap and PAGER, alerts and delivery partners), a tsunami warning center (messages, upgrades and cancellations) and a geological survey (debris-flow and ground failure hazard assessments, post-fire rainfall thresholds). Products carry the numbers a specialist checks: moment magnitude and MMI intensity are never interchanged, an alert level always travels with its aviation color code, and early warning can arrive after shaking near the epicenter.

vocabulary.public: residents in shaking, ashfall, lahar and tsunami hazard zones, school children, visitors and the aviation public
vocabulary.frontline: duty seismologists, volcano monitoring scientists, early warning operators, tsunami duty scientists, field geologists
vocabulary.operationsCenter: the observatory or network operations room and the partner emergency operations center

ShakeMap, PAGER and aftershock forecast production

roles.name: Scientist-in-Charge (volcano observatory)
roles.description: Volcano observatory variant. Owns the volcano alert level and aviation color code, statements and partner calls.

roles.name: Volcano Monitoring Scientist (deformation, gas, seismic)
roles.description: Volcano observatory variant. Interprets unrest data and recommends alert changes.

roles.name: Duty Seismologist
roles.description: Seismic network variant. Owns event locations and magnitudes, reviews automatic solutions and felt reports.

roles.name: Early Warning Operations Lead
roles.description: Early warning variant. Owns system health, alert review after events and the false alert response.

roles.name: Tsunami Warning Duty Scientist
roles.description: Tsunami warning center variant. Owns message type and areas, upgrades and cancellation.

roles.name: Landslide / Geologic Hazards Geologist
roles.description: Geological survey variant. Owns debris-flow hazard maps, rainfall thresholds and post-event reconnaissance.

roles.name: Network and Telemetry Engineer
roles.description: All variants. Owns station uptime, telemetry links, time sources and data latency.

roles.name: Hazard Communication / Public Affairs Officer
roles.team: Team H: Partners and Public Information
roles.description: All variants. Owns public statements, media, social posts and partner briefings.

roles.name: Emergency Management Liaison
roles.team: Team H: Partners and Public Information
roles.description: All variants. Joins emergency operations center calls and translates the science into decisions.

roles.name: Post-Earthquake Building Inspector Lead

outsideParties: USGS national centers (earthquake information, volcano hazards)
the National Weather Service (rainfall forecasts, tsunami dissemination)
early warning app and phone delivery partners
mediaChannels: a resident's post on Facebook or Nextdoor saying the shaking was felt
a post on X/Twitter with a fake tsunami video
the regional TV station's breaking news banner
a messaging group of parents at a school

sceneAnchors.control: inside a seismic network operations room: wall of waveform displays and map screens, two duty scientists at desks with headsets, fluorescent light

addedThreatFamilies.label: Earthquake
addedThreatFamilies.description: A damaging earthquake: the first automatic solution, the ShakeMap and PAGER estimates, lifeline and building damage, an aftershock sequence with its forecast, and re-entry decisions. Includes early warning that reaches phones seconds before the shaking, or fails to.

phaseArc.title: Shaking and First Information
phaseArc.goal: Seconds to minutes: an alert that arrives early, late or not at all, and first information that is incomplete and revised.
beats: An early warning alert (or the lack of one) on phones and an automated action log (trains slow, elevators stop)
The first automatic solution, with a magnitude that is revised within minutes, and the first felt reports
A noise item unrelated to the event (a non-seismic vibration report)
The ShakeMap and PAGER estimate appear, with a color level and an uncertain loss range

phaseArc.title: Damage and Lifelines
phaseArc.goal: The first hours: damage reports arrive unevenly and communications are strained.
beats: Time jump: field reports of damaged buildings, a collapsed overpass or a gas leak
A red herring: a report from a place the ShakeMap shows lightly shaken
Lifeline status (power, water, gas, roads, rail) reported by partners
A reporter wants to know whether this was the big one
A partner asks the scientists for a statement about aftershocks

phaseArc.title: Aftershocks and Forecast
phaseArc.goal: Days: the aftershock sequence continues and the forecast has to be explained without false comfort or false alarm.
beats: The aftershock forecast with probabilities for the next day, week and month
A large aftershock rattles damaged buildings; a rumor that a larger quake is coming
The decision point: re-occupy or keep closed damaged buildings and facilities while aftershocks continue
Building inspectors apply safety placards at a pace the demand outruns

phaseArc.title: Re-entry and Recovery
phaseArc.goal: Inspections, repairs and the return to service.
beats: Placard disputes and a facility that wants to re-open
A lifeline restored in stages; a hurdle that delays the last piece
After-action questions about warning timing and public messaging, then ENDEX

decisionPointExamples: re-occupy a damaged hospital wing or school now, or keep it closed while aftershocks continue
issue a statement that a larger earthquake is unlikely (probabilities are low but not zero) or stay silent while rumors spread
take an automated action on an early warning alert that may be a false alarm (stop trains, open doors) or wait for confirmation that arrives after the shaking
shut the gas line to a neighborhood for inspection or keep service on and accept the leak risk
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a revised magnitude, a ShakeMap intensity value at a named place, a PAGER color level, a station outage, a felt-report cluster, a lifeline status line
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: a damaged road that blocks inspectors, power loss at a monitoring station, a delivery partner that did not receive the alert, a building the placard system cannot cover in time
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the state or county emergency manager and the seismic network or USGS earthquake information center
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Magnitude is moment magnitude (Mw) and intensity is the Modified Mercalli scale (MMI, Roman numerals I to XII; USGS ShakeMap shows I to X+); never swap or mix them. The first magnitude is revised, usually within minutes. A forecast of aftershock probability is a probability, never a prediction of a date.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Volcanic unrest and eruption
addedThreatFamilies.description: A volcano moves from background to unrest, perhaps to eruption: rising seismicity, deformation and gas, alert level changes with aviation color codes, ash for aviation, lahars and flows, and the return to background.

phaseArc.title: Background and Unrest
phaseArc.goal: Ambiguity: monitoring data change slowly and nobody wants to say eruption is possible.
beats: A small increase in earthquake rate flagged by the monitoring scientist
A tourist reports a sulfur smell; a noise item unrelated to the volcano
A deformation or gas reading that is above background but within past ranges

phaseArc.title: Alert Level Changes
phaseArc.goal: The decision to raise the alert level and the aviation color code, and to coordinate the statement with emergency management and aviation.
beats: Time jump: swarm intensity increases and deformation accelerates
A red herring: a webcam image of steam that is weather cloud
The decision point: raise the alert level and color code now or wait for another data point
A Volcano Observatory Notice for Aviation and a notice to emergency management
A school district asks whether to cancel classes

phaseArc.title: Eruption, Ash and Lahars
phaseArc.goal: An eruption sends ash into airspace and flows down valleys; evacuation is timed by travel times.
beats: Eruption onset confirmed by seismic and infrasound data and a pilot report
A volcanic ash advisory and an aviation SIGMET; airport closures
A lahar warning and siren activation with a travel time to downstream communities
Misinformation about ash toxicity and drinking water

phaseArc.title: Waning and Re-entry
phaseArc.goal: Activity declines; returning to lower levels without false comfort.
beats: Activity wanes and the alert level is lowered in steps
Ash cleanup and water system questions
Re-entry of evacuated areas, then ENDEX

decisionPointExamples: raise the volcano alert level and aviation color code now, with the cost of a false alarm, or wait and risk being late
recommend evacuation of the lahar hazard zone on unrest alone or wait for eruption onset with only the travel time left
lower the alert level after activity wanes, or hold it to avoid a second round of confusion
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a seismicity rate, a tilt or GPS deformation reading, a gas flux measurement, a webcam image, a pilot report, an infrasound detection
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: a telemetry link lost to snow or ash, a station buried, a flight route that cannot be re-planned, a siren that does not sound
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the county emergency manager, aviation weather and the Volcanic Ash Advisory Center
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: A volcano alert level (Normal, Advisory, Watch, Warning) always travels with its aviation color code (Green, Yellow, Orange, Red). They usually pair in that order, but they are set separately: a hazardous eruption with little ash, such as a lava flow, is Warning with Orange. A Volcano Activity Notice announces an alert level change and a VONA announces a color code change. Alert levels can go up without an eruption. A lahar can reach communities hours after an eruption, or with no eruption at all.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Tsunami
addedThreatFamilies.description: A tsunami from a local source (minutes to the first wave) or a distant source (hours): the first message, upgrades or cancellation, waves and inundation, evacuation and the all clear.

phaseArc.title: Source Event
phaseArc.goal: A trigger that the warning center must interpret quickly with little data.
beats: A strong earthquake felt along the coast, or a distant event reported by the warning center
The first tsunami message with a threat level and an uncertain estimate
A noise item unrelated to the event

phaseArc.title: Messages and Decisions
phaseArc.goal: Message levels, upgrades and the decision to order evacuation while arrival times count down.
beats: Time jump: more data arrive; the message level is upgraded or downgraded
A fake video of a wave circulates before any real wave
The decision point: order the evacuation of a zone now for a local source, with minutes left
Ports, harbors and ferries decide to move vessels or hold them

phaseArc.title: Waves and Inundation
phaseArc.goal: The first waves arrive; observations arrive from tide gauges and buoys.
beats: First wave arrival time at a tide gauge, with an amplitude lower or higher than modeled
Later waves larger than the first; a person goes back to the shore to look
A road to high ground is blocked
Cancellation timing pressure from business and residents

phaseArc.title: All Clear and Recovery
phaseArc.goal: Cancellation is a decision, then damage assessment.
beats: The warning is cancelled or downgraded; the local all clear is the local authority's decision
Damage assessment of harbors and waterfront
Re-entry of evacuated zones, then ENDEX

decisionPointExamples: order evacuation of the inundation zone immediately for a local source, or wait for confirmation that costs minutes
upgrade an advisory to a warning when the first gauge reading arrives, or hold the level
cancel the warning when waves decline, or hold it because later waves can be larger
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a tide gauge record, a buoy reading, a travel time estimate, a first wave observation, a warning center message
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: a siren that does not sound, an evacuation route cut by earthquake damage, a message that does not reach a dissemination partner, a harbor with vessels that cannot leave
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the NOAA tsunami warning center and the county emergency manager
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Local sources give minutes, not hours; the first message may come before the first wave and the warning center cannot know the amplitude yet. A watch is not sent as a Wireless Emergency Alert. The local all clear belongs to local officials, not the warning center.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Post-fire debris flow
addedThreatFamilies.description: Rain on a burn scar produces debris flows with little warning: the hazard assessment, a rainfall threshold, a forecast storm, closures and evacuations, the flow and the clearing.

phaseArc.title: Fire and Hazard Assessment
phaseArc.goal: The fire is out; the hazard is not.
beats: A hazard assessment summary with probabilities and volumes for design storms
A question from a county about which roads are at risk
A noise item unrelated to the burn area

phaseArc.title: Forecast Storm
phaseArc.goal: A rain forecast crosses the threshold and officials must decide on closures and evacuations before it arrives.
beats: Time jump: a forecast with rainfall rates near the threshold
A red herring: a forecast that moves away and then back
The decision point: close the highway and order evacuations before the storm or wait for more certainty
The transportation department and the sheriff coordinate closures

phaseArc.title: Flows
phaseArc.goal: Debris flows start in minutes after intense rain; communications and rescue.
beats: A rain gauge in the burn area reports intensity above the threshold
A debris flow reported across a road; vehicles caught
A bridge or culvert blocked; stream rise downstream
Social media pictures with misattributed locations

phaseArc.title: Clearing and Re-opening
phaseArc.goal: Clearing debris, re-opening, and the next storm.
beats: Debris clearing priorities
The decision to reopen a road before the next storm
After-action review, then ENDEX

decisionPointExamples: close a highway and order evacuations before a forecast storm that may fizzle, or keep the highway open and accept the risk
re-open a cleared road before the next storm or keep it closed another day
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a rain gauge reading in the burn area, a rainfall forecast, a hazard map class, a field report of flow
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: a closed road that blocks equipment, a gauge that fails, a culvert filled by debris, a notice that does not reach residents
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the National Weather Service forecast office and the county emergency manager
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Debris flows are triggered by short, intense rainfall (rates over 15 minutes or an hour) on recent burns, not by total rainfall. Assessments give probability, volume and combined hazard for named storm intensities. Hazard maps are guidance for planning, not a forecast of a flow on a given day.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Ground failure after an earthquake
addedThreatFamilies.description: Liquefaction and earthquake-triggered landslides: the likelihood summaries, reports of lateral spreading, slides on roads and rail, and what the models cannot say about a single site.

phaseArc.title: Shaking and Model Output
phaseArc.goal: Ground failure models give likelihood areas before any report arrives.
beats: A ground failure summary with landslide and liquefaction likelihood classes
A first report of a road slide that matches the model
A noise item unrelated to ground failure

phaseArc.title: Reports and Closures
phaseArc.goal: Field reports contradict or confirm the model; routes close.
beats: Time jump: a rail line and a highway have slides; a report of sand boils at a port
A red herring: a report from a low-likelihood area
The decision point: close a route that the model puts in a low class but the field says is failing
Utilities report pipe breaks in liquefaction areas

phaseArc.title: Assessment and Response
phaseArc.goal: Geologists assess; agencies prioritize.
beats: A geologist visits a slope and advises on an evacuation below it
A school or hospital sits in a liquefaction area
Public questions about whether their home site is safe

phaseArc.title: Recovery
phaseArc.goal: Stabilization and re-opening.
beats: Slope stabilization and monitoring
Re-opening of routes with restrictions, then ENDEX

decisionPointExamples: close a route the model rates low but a field report says is failing, or keep it open
evacuate the homes below an unstable slope tonight, or wait for a geologist who cannot arrive until morning
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a ground failure likelihood class, a field report of a crack or slide, an inclinometer or monitoring reading
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: a slope too unstable for a survey crew, an access road buried, a monitoring instrument destroyed
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the state geological survey and the transportation department
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Ground failure model output is regional likelihood, not a statement about one site; say so whenever a summary is shown.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Monitoring or alerting degradation
addedThreatFamilies.description: The monitoring and warning systems themselves fail or err: a network or telemetry outage during unrest, a false early warning alert, a missed alert, a delayed or wrong tsunami message.

phaseArc.title: Something Is Off
phaseArc.goal: A symptom: stations drop out or an alert appears that no one expected.
beats: A set of stations goes quiet, or an alert appears for an earthquake nobody felt
An unrelated noise item
A first system status note that is ambiguous

phaseArc.title: Scope and Decision
phaseArc.goal: How bad is the loss of data and who must be told?
beats: Time jump: more stations fail; unrest at a volcano is now monitored by fewer instruments
A red herring: a second alert from a test message
The decision point: send a correction and retract the alert now or wait to confirm it was false
Partners ask whether automated actions fired

phaseArc.title: Impact and Messaging
phaseArc.goal: Consequences of the false or missed alert reach the public.
beats: Trains stopped by a false alert; a hospital activates its plan
Media and officials demand an explanation with a deadline
Misinformation that the system is unreliable and should be turned off

phaseArc.title: Recovery and Trust
phaseArc.goal: Restore data and explain.
beats: Repair crews restore telemetry
A review of the cause and a public statement
Partner agreements to re-enable automated actions, then ENDEX

decisionPointExamples: retract a possibly false alert immediately, or wait to confirm and let it stand
keep the volcano alert level where it is despite losing half the monitoring stations, or raise it because the data are incomplete
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a station health log line, a telemetry latency graph, an alert delivery receipt, a partner report of an action taken
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: a link repair that needs a helicopter, a vendor with a long response time, a delivery partner that cannot confirm what was sent
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the alert delivery partners and the emergency managers who depend on the alerts
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: A false alert and a missed alert have different harms. Corrections go out through the same channels and as fast as the original. Alerts near the epicenter can arrive after the shaking starts; this is a limit of the physics, not a failure.

noiseExamples: a quarry blast reported as an earthquake
a request for the school's earthquake drill certificate
a hiker asking whether the volcano trail is open
an expired software license on a field laptop
a student asking for a classroom visit
pressureExamples: a county commissioner asking whether to cancel a festival
a reporter asking the observatory whether the volcano is about to erupt
an airline operations center asking for the ash height now
a port director asking for the all clear
a school superintendent asking whether to evacuate students
a utility asking whether it must shut off gas in the whole city
